pages.title: What this unit is about
pages.body:
> 🌐 **Strand 3 — Communication Networks**
Sub-strand 1: Computer Networks

When you send a WhatsApp message to a friend in Bolgatanga, it travels through many connected devices, cables and radio links in a fraction of a second. These connected devices form networks. In this unit you will learn the hardware used to build networks, how devices can be arranged (topologies), the types of network by size, and how networking creates business opportunities.

pages.title: Content standard and lessons
pages.body:
> 🎯 **Content standard**
- **B7.3.1.1** Identify the concept of computer networking for global communications.

> 🧭 **What you will be able to do**
- **B7.3.1.1.1** Draw diagrams to illustrate features of the network topologies (Bus, Star, Ring, Mesh).
- **B7.3.1.1.2** Describe types of networks (PAN, LAN, MAN, WAN).
- **B7.3.1.1.3** Discuss the entrepreneurial opportunities in networking computing devices.

> 🗺️ **Lessons in this unit**
- 7.1 Network Hardware and Network Topologies
- 7.2 Types of Networks
- 7.3 Entrepreneurial Opportunities in Networking

**Core competencies developed:** Creativity and Innovation (CI6.1, CI6.6), Digital Literacy (DL5.1, DL5.4).

pages.title: Network Hardware and Network Topologies
Key network hardware
pages.body:
## Key network hardware
| **Hardware** | **Description and function** |
|---|---|
| Server | A powerful computer that provides services to other computers, e.g. storing shared files (file server), managing printing (print server), hosting websites (web server) or email (mail server). |
| Client | A computer or device that requests and uses services from a server, e.g. a learner’s computer in the lab. |
| Network Interface Card (NIC) | A circuit board or chip that allows a device to connect to a network; each has a unique **MAC address**. It may be wired (Ethernet port) or wireless (Wi-Fi adapter). |
| Hub | A simple device that connects several computers. It sends every message it receives to **all** connected devices, which wastes bandwidth. Now largely replaced by switches. |
| Switch | Connects devices in a LAN and sends each message **only** to the device it is meant for, making the network faster and more secure. |
| Router | Connects **different networks** together (e.g. the school LAN to the Internet) and chooses the best path for data. |
| Modem | Converts digital computer signals into signals that can travel over telephone lines, cable or mobile networks, and back again (MOdulator–DEModulator). Home “Wi-Fi routers” often combine modem, router, switch and access point in one box. |
| Wireless Access Point (WAP) | Lets wireless devices join a wired network using Wi-Fi. |
| Cables | **Twisted-pair (Ethernet) cable** with RJ-45 plugs (most common in LANs); **coaxial cable** (cable TV); **fibre-optic cable**, which carries data as pulses of light: very fast, long distances, immune to electrical interference (used by Internet backbones and undersea cables). |

pages.title: Key network hardware (continued)
pages.body:
> 🇬🇭 **Ghana connection — Undersea cables** Ghana connects to the rest of the world’s Internet through several undersea fibre-optic cables that land on our coast, such as **SAT-3**, **WACS**, **MainOne**, **Glo-1** and **ACE**. In March 2024, damage to some of these cables off the West African coast slowed Internet services in Ghana and neighbouring countries for days, which shows how much our daily lives depend on network hardware.
## Network topologies
A **topology** is the layout or arrangement of devices (called **nodes**) and the connections between them.
[[fig:c7-f16|Figure 15: Bus, star, ring and mesh topologies]]

pages.title: Key network hardware (continued)
pages.body:
| **Topology** | **Features** | **Advantages** | **Disadvantages** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bus | All devices connect to one main cable (the **backbone**) with a **terminator** at each end to stop signals bouncing back. Data travels along the backbone and every device sees it. | Cheap and easy to set up; uses the least cable | If the backbone breaks, the whole network fails; slows down as more devices are added; collisions; hard to find faults |
| Star | Every device has its own cable to a **central switch or hub**. All data passes through the centre. | If one cable fails, only that device is affected; easy to add devices and find faults; good performance with a switch | If the central switch fails, the network stops; uses more cable than bus |
| Ring | Each device connects to exactly two others, forming a **closed loop**. Data travels in one direction (or both in a dual ring), passing from device to device. Some ring networks use a **token** that is passed round to control who may send. | No collisions; performs well under heavy load; equal access for all devices | A break in the ring or a failed device can stop the whole network (unless dual ring); adding devices disrupts the network |
| Mesh | Devices have **multiple connections** to each other. In a **full mesh**, every device connects to every other device; in a **partial mesh**, only some do. | Very reliable: if one link fails, data takes another route; handles heavy traffic | Expensive and complex; uses a lot of cable; a full mesh with n devices needs n(n − 1) ÷ 2 links |

pages.title: Key network hardware (continued)
pages.body:
> ✏️ **Worked example — Counting links in a full mesh**
With **5** computers: 5 × (5 − 1) ÷ 2 = 5 × 4 ÷ 2 = **10** cables. With **10** computers: 10 × 9 ÷ 2 = **45** cables. This is why full mesh is rarely used for large LANs, although the Internet itself is a giant **partial mesh**.
> ✨ **Did you know?** Most school and office LANs today use a **star** topology built around switches. Several stars are often linked together to form a **hybrid (tree)** topology.
> 🧪 **Activity — Draw and present**
In groups, draw well-labelled diagrams of the four topologies on chart paper. Under each diagram, list two features, two advantages and two disadvantages. Present your diagrams to the class, then watch a short video on network topologies and add anything new you learnt. Finally, identify the topology used in your school’s computer lab.

pages.title: Types of Networks
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B7.3.1.1.2
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- explain PAN, LAN, WLAN, MAN, WAN and the Internet;
- give examples of each type of network.
Networks are often classified by the **geographical area** they cover.
[[fig:c7-f17|Figure 16: Types of networks by geographical coverage]]
| **Type** | **Coverage** | **Examples** | **Typical technology** |
|---|---|---|---|
| PAN – Personal Area Network | Around one person, about 10 metres | Phone connected to wireless earbuds, a smartwatch or a car; phone sharing files with a laptop | Bluetooth, USB, NFC |
| LAN – Local Area Network | A single building or site | School computer lab, office, Internet café, home network | Ethernet cables and switches; Wi-Fi |
| WLAN – Wireless LAN | A LAN without cables | Wi-Fi in a hotel, airport or school | Wi-Fi access points |
| MAN – Metropolitan Area Network | A city or large town | Connecting all branches of a bank or all campuses of a university across Accra or Kumasi; city CCTV networks | Fibre-optic cables, microwave links |
| WAN – Wide Area Network | Countries and continents | A bank’s national network linking branches in all regions; telecom networks | Fibre, satellite, undersea cables, leased lines |
| The Internet | The whole world | Millions of networks linked together (a global WAN) | All of the above |

pages.title: Types of Networks (continued)
pages.body: > 🎯 **BECE focus** A **Metropolitan Area Network (MAN)** connects local networks across a larger geographical region such as a city. Remember the order of size: **PAN < LAN < MAN < WAN**.

pages.title: Entrepreneurial Opportunities in Networking
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B7.3.1.1.3
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- discuss the benefits and challenges of networking in different environments;
- identify where each type of network is applied;
- identify ways networking can be turned into a business.
## Benefits and challenges of networks in different environments
| **Environment** | **Benefits** | **Challenges** |
|---|---|---|
| School | Share printers, Internet and learning materials; central storage of learners’ work; e-learning platforms | Cost of equipment; need for a technician; misuse of the Internet; viruses spreading |
| Business | Share customer data and stock records across branches; email and video meetings; online sales; Mobile Money payments | Cyber attacks; data loss; downtime affects sales; installation and data costs |
| Health | Patient records shared between departments and hospitals; telemedicine; quick access to laboratory results | Patient privacy must be protected; network failure can delay treatment |
| Home | Share Internet among phones, TVs and laptops; smart devices; online learning | Data costs; children’s online safety |

pages.title: Turning networking into a business
pages.body:
## Turning networking into a business
Networking skills create many **entrepreneurial** (business) opportunities, which means you can create your own job:
- **Network installation and cabling:** wiring schools, offices, hotels and churches with structured cabling and Wi-Fi.
- **Network maintenance and support:** offering monthly support contracts to small businesses.
- **Internet café and printing/photocopy centres** near schools and offices.
- **Wi-Fi hotspot business:** selling Wi-Fi access vouchers in markets, hostels or lorry stations.
- **CCTV and smart-security installation** using IP cameras on a network.
- **Selling and repairing network equipment:** routers, cables, phones and accessories.
- **Training:** teaching networking and computer skills to others.
- **Online businesses** that depend on networks: e-commerce shops, digital marketing, web hosting.
> 💡 **Career Corner** Careers in networking include **network technician**, **network administrator**, **network engineer**, **cybersecurity analyst** and **cloud engineer**. Professional certificates such as **CompTIA Network+** and **Cisco CCNA** can lead to jobs in telecom companies, banks and the civil service.
> 🧪 **Activity — Business plan pitch**
In groups, choose one networking business idea. Prepare a short pitch covering: the service, the customers in your community, the equipment needed, a rough start-up cost in GH₵, and two challenges with solutions. Present it to the class “investors” (your classmates), who vote for the best idea.

pages.title: Review: written and practical tasks
pages.body:
> ✏️ **Review exercises** — answer these in your exercise book or on the computer, then check with your teacher.
## Short answer questions
1. Define a computer network and state **three** benefits of networking.
2. Explain the functions of a server, a client, a switch and a router.
3. With the aid of diagrams, describe the bus and ring topologies.
4. Compare the star and mesh topologies in terms of reliability and cost.
5. Distinguish between a LAN and a WAN, giving an example of each.
6. Describe **four** business opportunities in networking.
## Practical tasks
1. Visit your school’s computer lab with your teacher and identify the switch, router, cables and access points. Draw a diagram of the lab network and name its topology.
